inquiries.inquiry: Our founding gathering - establishing the Lyceum
inquiries.quote: An endeavor for shared purpose in families and communities.
inquiries.callToAction: First circle: we agreed on the rules, norms, and the Sequence of Inquiry that every gathering since has followed.

inquiries.inquiry: What should we strive for in a modern work ethic?
How can we help families afford housing in their communities?
How do we mentor adolescents (15+) into legal adulthood?
How do we cultivate peaceful co-existence with nature within our communities?
How can we embody the values of a humanitarian in our communities?
How can we advocate for healthcare equity in our communities?
What should leaders do to empower education and communities?
inquiryAliases: What should leaders do to empower education in communities?

meeting.landAcknowledgement: No spoken land acknowledgement was given; the opening was a breathing exercise with gratitude prompts for the Earth, ancestors, self, family, and the next generation. Marcia Lopez typed gratitude in the chat for living and learning on the stolen lands of the Squamish, Tsleil-Waututh and Musqueam Nations, and Larry added that he grew up in Ocean County, New Jersey learning about the Lenape. Canada's land acknowledgement practice and the Truth and Reconciliation Commission were later discussed as an example of a country teaching a fuller history.

Pre-survey learning conversation, by QR code or a link in the chat
Opening presence exercise: guided breaths with gratitude prompts
Shared understanding round on background, cultural background, family, and connection to the Lyceum
World map orientation using United Nations and World Bank regional maps
Sequence of Inquiry: choosing a topic by consensus, then working it through

contextNotes: Scheduled for about an hour and a half as an open forum; participants free to come and go.
Held online across Canada and the United States, from Vancouver to Pittsburgh.
Two participants attended their first Lyceum and were welcomed as new guests.
Topic was chosen in the circle rather than set in advance.
Two candidate topics emerged; leadership and national messaging was set aside for education.
Discussion followed the March 2025 move to dismantle the United States Department of Education.
Sequence of Inquiry ran theories, application, shared understanding, opportunities and challenges, and call to action.
One participant shared a room and connection with another, so the transcript labels her speech as his.
Land gratitude was typed in the chat rather than spoken aloud.
A participant's young child appeared briefly on camera during introductions and did not speak.
Participants stepped away and returned mid-session; one stepped away near the close and did not speak again.
Chat carried content the audio did not, including the land gratitude and a closing point on non-traditional educators.
Recording began about six minutes after the meeting, so chat timestamps run ahead of the recording clock.
Next Lyceum announced for the following month, with a six-month reflection on open inquiries.

theories.text: Canada's federal government stopped funding housing for people without means in the nineties.
Public school facilities and equipment show degradation, unlike the federally funded schools.
Chile offers three school routes: public, part-subsidized, and private, the middle most sought.
The Department of Education was a back-office body with little influence on schools.
Left to their own devices, states might not do what serves America best.
Federal grants and priorities reinforced underserved communities at primary and secondary level.
Schools testing better on standardized tests receive more money, compounding the gap.
With no national curriculum, competing ideas of the nation leave no common identity.
Federal funding compensates underserved communities underfinanced by tax and property based systems.
Inequality once formed may take two or three generations to rebalance.
Desegregation of schools happened for the students but not for the teachers.
Programs a nation runs show what that country places most value on.
Part of an education can come from adults who are not technically educators.
A federal government withdrawing from provision leaves communities carrying it, housing then education.
Sorting by money and address reproduces the segregation that law has already ended.

applications.text: El Paso - the local independent district ran the on-post school, 99 percent military students.
Department of Defense schools on post - new smart boards and almost unlimited resources.
A private Christian school funded by tuition enrollment and parent volunteering.
Chile - three school options; the subvencion middle takes state money, families pay half.
Gratuidad - Chile lets students with strong results attend university free of charge, while ordinary fees stand at about the minimum wage. Name from the foundation's notes, not spoken in the session.
Alabama - the National Guard was mobilized over the state's hold on segregated schools.
Texas - an added district fee transfers a child out of a Title I school.
China and South Korea - placement schools drill students for make-or-break entrance exams.
Japan and Australia - a national curriculum the ministry sets and prefectures tailor locally.
Virginia SOL and Texas STAAR - each state sets its own standards and testing.
A federal STEM priority program, prompted by Sputnik, fostered state standards.
Pittsburgh - desegregated in law in 1981, with a high school sited between two suburbs as the remedy rather than the source of the bias.
Desegregation integrated the students but not the teachers; African American teachers were fired.
Canada - no federal oversight of education; every province runs its own.
International Baccalaureate programs sited in the lowest ranked high schools.
Teachers receive a stipend for working at schools with certain populations.
Homeschooling - math applied while buying things at the store, cooking as a class.
Land acknowledgement - naming the First Nations, Metis and Inuit peoples who came before.
Austria and Germany - almost anyone in the street can answer a question in English.
International agencies grant credit hours for education earned in another country.

Some level of standard, so all of the next generation gets equal access.
An accounting of whether money saved by disestablishment reaches schools and states.
Federal partner agencies whose interagency work gives visibility into education programs.
Federal overarching guidance on curriculum, or at least a federal standard.

Church and community organizations as a channel to families inside the school system.
A Malcolm Gladwell book on Ivy League schools and what culture says about education.
Clear standards for homeschooling, unknown in the arrangements seen in other homes.
Teachers themselves as a source on stipends and why staff choose a school.
A curriculum and specialty for English as a second language.
Levelling adult language provision, so long-settled newcomers can reach college.
A route for citizens and parents to shape the curriculum their children see.
A degree and thesis in human development already inside the group.
Migrant women's groups as a source on the newcomer experience.
Need for fiscal transparency: the department's budget, the claimed savings, and what reaches a student.
Need to establish who inherits each department function and who enforces equal access.
Need a plain account of what the department actually governs and administers.
Need to know what happens to special education and accessibility duties tied to federal grants.
Need to test whether reported school scores measure the school or the program placed in it.
Need first-hand accounts from teachers, parents and community groups, not news coverage alone.
Need a comparison of how other countries hold a standard without a federal department.
Need to map how curriculum is decided, and where parents and citizens can enter.
Need one national standard for what every state teaches, and equal access to it.
Need visible standards behind homeschooling, and support for the families choosing it.
Need education that closes the gap when a newcomer's credentials stop counting.

Need evidence on who teaches where, and how pay and placement shape it.

policies.text: Department of Education charter: equal access to education for all American students.
Department of Education created about 1979 to affirm equal attention across districts.
United States moves to dissolve the Department of Education.
Department remit named: teachers union influence, student loans, funding for some schools.
Schools taking federal support must enforce equal opportunity and nondiscrimination standards.
Special education programs meeting set criteria required of federal grant recipients.
Federal government has not participated in education standards, with one exception.
Soviet Sputnik launch preceded the first American space vehicle.

National Defense Education Act - the Sputnik-era federal STEM priority later housed in the Education Department, which fostered state standards. Name from the foundation's notes, not spoken in the session.

Section 256 - the 'separate but equal' provision behind Alabama's segregated schools, named in the circle as a familiar term that was never true. Name from the foundation's notes, not spoken in the session.
Alabama - National Guard mobilized over the state's hold on school segregation.
A high school placed between two suburbs to force new district lines.
IRS and Department of Defense cited as programs showing national priorities.
Canada's Truth and Reconciliation Commission, instituted to address a gap in history.
Land acknowledgement of First Nations history now a mandate taught nationwide.

opportunities.text: Home-based homeschool programs seen running very successfully, with children thriving.
Homeschooling frees a family to travel or finish the year early.
Communities could introduce the morals, ethics and cultural identity they value.
The dissolution debate has people talking about education and what matters.
Lyceum leans into the problem rather than political identity or ideology.
Education could help arriving professionals keep a similar quality of life.
Multilingual newcomers often speak three languages where critics barely speak one.
Later arrivals start from collected knowledge rather than from nothing.

challenges.text: Left to their own devices, states may not serve the national interest.
Open forum means participants step away mid-inquiry and miss part of it.
Shutdown costs end up exceeding the cost of continuing the programs.
Money left over after closures will not be put back into education.
Empowering states enables retrogression on equal opportunity and non-discrimination.
Families who can afford the transfer send children to the better school.
Schools that lose students slide into outdated textbooks and worn furniture.
Curriculum gaps between states leave transferring students playing catch up.
Effects of eliminating programs ripple back slowly, like a pebble in water.
Minority students may have no teacher who looks like them to look up to.
Dissolving the department may show education is valued less than assumed.
Growing move to homeschooling driven by dissatisfaction with schooling offered.
Special programs placed to change the statistics reported to the federal government.
Rumors of bad influences and negative peer groups raise safety concerns.
Without a basis for morals and ethics, conduct becomes a free for all.
Communities left to address inequalities with no federal resourcing or support.
Credentials do not transfer: a lawyer at home ends up cleaning houses.
Without the language, newcomers cannot enter university, college or other learning.
A country that claims not to be racist can still hold much racism.

inquiries.quote: The child that doesn't get educated may be the one that can cure the common cold, but we don't know that because we didn't educate him or her.
inquiries.callToAction: Rachel Gruber volunteered to carry the inquiry forward, taking up how curriculum is developed and whether citizens and parents can be given a voice in what their children are taught in school. Ehren Gruber joined her immediately, said the team was not limited to two, and undertook to build a shared product the group can add to and circulate as more people become interested. Hez Jenkins volunteered to take part as well. The recording names four people on the inquiry team; one of them was not present at the gathering, so the record carries three named stewards and one further steward, withheld. Ehren Gruber also offered to follow up with a participant whose community work supports newcomer women, to learn from that experience for the inquiry. Larry proposed in the chat that the group take up further discussion on the topic, and Ehren Gruber accepted it into the six-month reflection, where the circle revisits six inquiries and those carrying each one report back for questions and input. Ehren Gruber, Chase Kubic and Hez Jenkins, as hosts, will develop products from the session and be in touch afterwards, with the next Lyceum set for the following month.

storyboard.logline: A seven-person Lyceum spanning Vancouver, Virginia and Pittsburgh took a live news item, the dissolving of the US Department of Education, and turned it into one question about what leaders owe education in their own communities.
storyboard.arcNotes: The session followed its script and still turned twice. It opened tightly - rules and norms, a pre-survey called the learning conversation, a breathing circle with gratitude to the Earth, to ancestors, to self, to family and to the next generation - and the shared understanding round showed a circle that is largely one extended family, held together by military service as much as by blood, plus two first-time guests. The first turn came when the topic arrived from the floor: not education in the abstract but the dissolving of the US Department of Education, which handed the group a live case with a Canadian comparison already in the room. The middle hour stayed unusually factual for a Lyceum, with participants supplying what they had seen rather than what they believed: every school type in one military family's life, Chile's three routes with a part-subsidized middle, a reported department budget and how little of it reaches a student, the department's real charter of equal access, its grants and non-discrimination enforcement, and the single federal intervention in standards after Sputnik. The second turn went inward, from policy to inheritance: Pittsburgh desegregated on paper in 1981 and not in fact, schools desegregated for students but not for teachers, a transfer fee that reopens sorting by income, International Baccalaureate programs sited to lift a weak school's reported scores, stipends that route teachers by need rather than fit. From there the circle asked what a government's national programs reveal about what it values, and answered that a community can decide morals, ethics and cultural identity for itself when the state will not. The last twenty minutes belonged to newcomers and to language: qualifications that stop counting at a border, language as both respect and gate, assimilation bought at the cost of a grandmother's German. The call to action was taken up rather than assigned - how curriculum is developed, and whether parents and citizens can have a voice in it - and the fellowship circle closed on the same theme from another angle, that much of the teaching that matters is done by people who are not teachers. Suppressions, all deliberate rather than accidental: three children's names withheld; the personal history of the two first-time guests withheld and their self-introductions attributed to a participant; one participant's account of immigration and of racism experienced attributed to a participant, with country and city removed; the names of four service colleagues and of two family members who were not in the room withheld, and with them a spouse's teaching anecdote and a spouse's credential story, whose substance is kept without them; a serving participant's pending relocation left out; a young child briefly on camera not recorded. Three stewards are named and a fourth, a family member who was never in the room, is withheld, so that list is one short on purpose. The chat log runs six minutes and twenty-six seconds ahead of the recording, and chat contributions are placed at their recording-clock equivalents. The title of the Malcolm Gladwell book is garbled in the source and is not corrected here.

beats.title: Norms, survey, and the presence circle
beats.summary: Ehren Gruber opened the Lyceum as an endeavor for shared purpose for families and communities, welcomed two new guests and ran an audio check with Al Goshi as he came on board. He set the norms: about an hour and a half, an open forum where people come and go as life dictates, hosted with Chase Kubic and Hez Jenkins, everyone a peer whatever their walk of life, difficult and sensitive topics approached with curiosity, commonality sought while difference is acknowledged. He walked the agenda and put up the pre-survey, called the learning conversation, by chat link or QR code, describing it as a way to ground where each person is emotionally and what they may need from the group. He then led the opening presence: turn sideways to open to the group and to the nature around it, lower the gaze, and five breaths, each with a prompt of gratitude.
beats.pullQuote: here, in this space, in the Lyceum we're all considered peers
beats.slideHint: Title slide 'Lyceum - an endeavor for shared purpose for families and communities' with rules and norms (peers, curiosity, commonality, open forum, hosts named), then an agenda strip, then the pre-survey QR code labeled Learning Conversation with a chat-link fallback, then a plain Presence slide listing the five gratitude prompts in order: Earth, ancestors, self, family and friends, the next generation.

beats.title: Shared understanding round
beats.summary: The circle went round on cultural background, family and connection to the Lyceum. Ehren Gruber gave a mixture of European and Asian descent, born and raised in the United States, now living in Vancouver, British Columbia, where his family took up community engagement locally. Larry introduced the European side of the family, born in America and living in Virginia, connected to everyone else through his son or through long friendship. Al Goshi was raised in Hawaii in a Japanese American community and claims Irish by marriage, and counts himself part of an extended family that reaches across three households. Hez Jenkins is serving in the military in Pittsburgh, originally from Texas, has been all over Europe and South Korea, homeschools his children, and came to the group through Chase Kubic, his former commander. Chase met Ehren in freshman year of high school and serves alongside Hez. Both first-time guests also introduced themselves; those introductions are recorded here as a participant and the personal detail in them is withheld. Ehren closed the round by restating that the forum is open and anyone who steps away will be brought back up to speed.
beats.pullQuote: Larry is my brother-in-law by military service and curmudgeonly perspective.
beats.slideHint: Shared Understanding slide with the three prompts small in the corner (cultural background, family composition, connection to the Lyceum) and a round-robin list of one line per person, the two guest lines left as 'guest' with a footnote that a first-time guest's personal detail is withheld from the record.

beats.title: A world map, and the question arrives
beats.summary: Ehren Gruber used the United Nations country map and a World Bank map that colors the world by region, suggesting the colors as a memory prompt so lived experience and cultural wisdom could be brought to bear on whatever the group chose. He explained the sequence of inquiry for the two newcomers: find a topic that matters to the group, build consensus on it, then work through theories, application in communities, what gets to the root, opportunities and challenges, and a call to action that somebody carries and reports back on, so the discussion becomes a quest rather than an evening. The floor opened. Rachel Gruber proposed the role of education in communities, prompted by moves to dissolve the US Department of Education, and asked what federal and state governments each do for educating youth, and what a state-led system loses without federal support. Marcia Lopez answered from Canada, where the federal government has not directly funded housing for people without means since the 1990s, and added a second worry, whether the US President's talk about Canada is a joke or serious.
beats.pullQuote: the role of education in our communities. In the Us. They're looking at dissolving the Department of education.
beats.slideHint: Two slides: the color-coded World Bank region map under 'consider where you have been and where you are now', then the Sequence of Inquiry ladder (topic by consensus, theories and concepts, application, root causes, opportunities and challenges, call to action) with a note that a call to action means somebody carries the inquiry and comes back with updates.

beats.title: Two candidate questions, and why community
beats.summary: Ehren Gruber drafted a question on screen and drew the parallel out loud: a federal government that once provided supportive housing withdrew from it, and a department the United States has relied on may go the same way. Two avenues sat on the table, education and leadership in how messages are conveyed across countries, and he invited the group to narrow either. He explained why the group keeps saying community: the Lyceum works at the scale of towns, cities, cultural and religious groups, not capitals, because that is where decisions land on families. Chase Kubic added the group's levels of impact, from individual to family to local community, with state and federal effect a longer-term goal, and argued that what shapes daily life is settled locally: taxes, housing, food and shelter, whether a big store closes, what the gas price is. On the first candidate question he admitted knowing the Department of Education only in outline, student loans, school nutrition, broad guidelines, and asked whether the leadership question could be narrowed before the group took it on.
beats.pullQuote: Now it starts to call into question, what does the government supposed to do, if anything, to empower education for communities.
beats.slideHint: Deliberation slide with the two candidate questions side by side and space to edit them live, next to a levels-of-impact diagram (individual, family, local community, state, federal) with the daily-life list beneath it: taxes, housing, food, shelter, local business, fuel prices.

beats.title: One question, chosen by consensus
beats.summary: Al Goshi proposed folding leadership into the education question rather than dropping either, while refusing to dismiss the question of whether the President is serious about making Canada the 51st state. He said he cannot always tell how seriously to take what is said, that a worst-case threat analysis discounts nothing, and that weakening and disestablishing the Education Department is a long-stated aim now coming true with major effect. Analyzing that stated vision against what is actually happening in US education policy would limit the scope of both candidate questions, he suggested, before wondering aloud whether the framing was too US-centric. Ehren Gruber asked twice for objections, a raised hand or a thumbs up, took the silence as consent, and set the evening's question, noting that leaders could mean education administrators or anyone providing educational services. The theories section then opened with what people have experienced of education in a community, public, private, government or vocational.
beats.pullQuote: Looking at the question as written, what should leaders do to empower education and communities
beats.slideHint: Today's Inquiry slide - 'What should leaders do to empower education in communities?' - with a definition strip widening leaders to administrators, education services and non-formal educators, and the sequence of inquiry down the side as the evening's roadmap.

beats.title: One family, every kind of school
beats.summary: Chase Kubic offered his own experience as the first theory: public elementary, middle and high school in Norfolk, Virginia, a public university left unfinished, then a second public institution with more private elements. As a parent he has seen a private Christian school funded by tuition, parent volunteering and small overheads, run by a board to a budget; a public district school serving an installation where about ninety-nine percent of students came from the military; and Department of Defense federal schools where the funding was visible in smart boards, screens, computers, integrated technology and modern buildings. Ordinary public schools showed the reverse, a degradation of facilities and equipment, with localities choosing very different shares of city or state budget to put into a school, a quarter in one place and half in another. He had also taught languages in post-secondary settings in other countries, which ran differently again, and he handed the question back to the group.
beats.pullQuote: So there's some major differences and some inconsistencies across the nation, at least, that I've seen
beats.slideHint: Theories and Concepts slide: a comparison table of school types (private religious, district school serving an installation, Department of Defense federal school, ordinary public school) scored on funding source, facilities, technology and oversight, with 'inconsistencies across the nation' as the banner line.

beats.title: Chile's three routes, and what the department does
beats.summary: Marcia Lopez set out the Chilean system: twelve years of school then college or university, with three routes to choose from. Public schooling, a part-subsidized category where the government funds the school and the family pays half, and private, with most families reaching for the middle option because it is the affordable one. Students with strong results can attend university free, which she called the good part of the system, while ordinary university fees stand near the minimum wage. Her own question stayed open, what actually happens in the United States if the ministry is dissolved and the responsibility passes to governors or municipalities. Chase Kubic answered with what he had followed in the news, unverified but widely reported: overarching guidelines touching nutrition, influence with the teachers union, administration of student loans and some school funding, a back-office department with little direct influence on schools, with curriculum left to city, county or state. He cited a budget figure near 286 billion dollars with roughly a quarter reaching individual students, and said the rest of it remains unknown, an evolving issue nobody outside the department can call.
beats.pullQuote: the school receives money and you pay half.
beats.slideHint: Application slide 'how is this handled elsewhere': Chile's three routes as three columns (public, part-subsidized with the family paying half, private) with free university on results called out, next to a panel on what the US Department of Education actually administers and the disputed budget figure marked as unverified.

beats.title: Equal access, and who watches the states
beats.summary: Larry named the department's real charter as equal access rather than dictation to local schools, and reached back to segregation, to Alabama holding so dearly to segregated schools that the National Guard was mobilized over it, and to the phrase separate yet equal, which he said was simply not true. Left to their own devices, he argued, states may not do what is in the country's interest, and the child who never gets educated may be the one who could have cured the common cold. He asked whether money saved by disestablishing the department will in fact cycle down to schools, states and local jurisdictions, and read Al Goshi's expression as one dissenting vote from the gentleman from Hawaii. Al agreed and set out the programs he sees through a federal department that cooperates with them: grants and priorities for underserved communities, enforced standards of equal opportunity and non-discrimination, special education criteria, developmental access, ramps and mobility devices. He argued that the claimed savings from shutdowns cost more than continuing the programs, that whatever remains will go to another pet project rather than back to education, and that empowering the states risks reversing fifty years of a common standard. Larry stepped away briefly, posting his thanks in the chat.
beats.pullQuote: The child that doesn't get educated may be the one that can cure the common cold, but we don't know that because we didn't educate him or her.
beats.slideHint: Sources and Inputs slide headed 'equal access is the charter': a list of the department's programs (grants to underserved schools, non-discrimination enforcement, special education criteria, physical access), a history strip (segregation, separate yet equal, the National Guard in Alabama), and a savings-versus-shutdown-cost pair of bars.

beats.title: Transfer fees, entrance exams, no national curriculum
beats.summary: Chase Kubic agreed the money would find another department rather than return to education, dated the department's creation to 1979 with a mandate for equal attention it has not fulfilled, and gave the mechanism he has used himself: in Texas a family that can pay an added district fee and drive their child can transfer out of a Title I school to any school they like. Those who can afford it choose the better school, its ratings keep improving, and a form of segregation persists, which he called disproportionate to the department's intent and mostly a state-level failure. Ehren Gruber widened the frame to China and South Korea, where entrance exams decide university places and later employment, and students study themselves almost to death for a score that can send a life either way. He then named the deeper gap: Japan and Australia teach a national curriculum and the United States does not, so history and what it means to be American are interpreted school by school, which he read as a national identity crisis underneath the polarization. Larry posted in the chat that this was the start of separate but equal.
beats.pullQuote: there's almost like there's a national identity crisis. It's like, Hey, what does it mean to be an American?
beats.slideHint: Two panels: 'shifting to the better school' with the added district fee, the ratings loop and the funding that follows the scores; and 'national curriculum' comparing Japan and Australia with the United States, with the entrance-exam cultures of China and South Korea shown as the extreme case of education deciding a life.

beats.title: State standards and one federal exception
beats.summary: Chase Kubic pointed to Virginia's Standards of Learning and the Texas STAAR tests as proof that standards are set state by state, and described the cost of moving between them: children arriving from a high-performing state ahead of the local curriculum, then playing catch-up after the next move, with one of his children losing a year of math placement in the process. He would prefer a national curriculum, or at least a federal standard, because states are being treated almost as separate countries. Al Goshi answered that the federal government has kept out of education standards exactly once: after the Soviet Union launched Sputnik, a STEM priority program eventually housed in the Education Department fostered state standards at primary, secondary and post-secondary level. Beyond that, the federal role has been to insist that whatever standard a state sets is equally accessible across its population, and to fund underserved communities where property-tax-based school finance falls short. Ehren Gruber tied this back to Larry's chat line about separate but equal, and warned that inequality, once formed, takes two or three generations to unwind.
beats.pullQuote: We're almost treating each State as a different country based on, you know, their own curriculum
beats.slideHint: Policies slide: a strip contrasting state testing regimes (Standards of Learning in Virginia, STAAR in Texas, Department of Defense schools in the middle) with a timeline callout for the post-Sputnik STEM program as the single federal intervention in standards, and a footnote on property-tax-based school funding.

beats.title: Pittsburgh, and what a government values
beats.summary: Hez Jenkins described Pittsburgh's particular case: legally desegregated in 1981, but the shape of the city and its suburbs left segregation standing, and a high school was placed between two suburbs to force new district lines, which people resented at the time and, he believes, resent still. Homeschooling his own children, he hears from church and community families about strong programs and troubled kids inside the same buildings, and warned that anything adopted now is a pebble dropped in water whose ripples take time to return. Rachel Gruber picked up the desegregation thread from a recent Malcolm Gladwell book on the Ivy League and what the culture says about education, its title garbled in the recording: schools were desegregated for students but not for teachers, African American teachers were largely dismissed, and minority students were left without a teacher who looked like them or saw things differently, an effect she said is still felt. That took her to what a government's national programs reveal about what it values, and to the worry that dissolving the department shows education is valued less than assumed. She noted Canada has no federal oversight of education at all; everything sits with the provinces.
beats.pullQuote: What? What does the Us. Government value? And it I feel like things that have a national program are kind of like showing what our country places most value on.
beats.slideHint: Root Causes slide: a Pittsburgh timeline (legal desegregation in 1981, a high school sited between two suburbs, tension that outlasted the order) beside a 'desegregated for students, not for teachers' panel, with the pebble-in-the-water image for lag time and a one-line comparison of where oversight sits in Canada and the United States.

beats.title: School districts, stipends, and homeschooling
beats.summary: Hez Jenkins relayed a teacher's account from a school on a base: staff could tell, without testing, whether a student arriving from a given state would be ahead or behind. Chase Kubic said his family chose their rented house for its school district, knowing which schools it fed before the move, and named a growing turn to homeschooling among families dissatisfied with what their children were getting, with quality varying sharply from one household to the next. He then described an engineered kind of sorting: International Baccalaureate programs placed in the lowest-ranked high school in each of three Virginia cities, which lifts that school's reported scores, and stipends that draw teachers to the most challenged schools, so that where a teacher works carries its own stigma or status. Hez set out why his family homeschools: safety, rumors about the next school, bad influences and peer groups, and a felt absence of structure in morals and ethics, alongside the freedom to travel and to substitute practical life learning, cooking, shopping, applying math in the shop, for book knowledge alone.
beats.pullQuote: So teachers, if they need money or they need to be paid more, are going to work at some of the the more challenged schools.
beats.slideHint: Challenges slide split three ways - choosing a home by school district, International Baccalaureate placement lifting a weak school's numbers, stipends and stigma following teachers - with a fourth column on homeschooling motives: safety, morals and ethics, flexibility, practical learning.

beats.title: Communities as curriculum
beats.summary: Ehren Gruber turned to opportunities. If education falls to states and communities, then morals and ethics need not be left to an institution to define, and the diversity of the United States means communities could shape cultural identity themselves, with Hispanic, Black, Asian, Jewish and other voices saying what their own heritage means. Chase Kubic argued that the pot has been stirred: immigration went almost unspoken until it was raised, education may be the same, and polarized argument beats stagnation if it reinvigorates the question of how to invest in children and at what level. Ehren replied that the Lyceum holds difficult conversations by leaning into the problem rather than into political identity or ideology, and offered Canada as a worked example, the land acknowledgement and a Truth and Reconciliation Commission he dated to 2016 making First Nations, Metis and Inuit history a taught mandate, filling a gap in the national story. Marcia Lopez posted her own gratitude in the chat for living and learning on the stolen lands of the Squamish, Tsleil-Waututh and Musqueam Nations. Chase then opened the language question: states with heavy immigration, a curriculum delivered in English, English as a second language, refugees arriving already at school age.
beats.pullQuote: We don't lean into ideology, we lean into the problem that exists.
beats.slideHint: Opportunities slide 'communities as curriculum': three bullets (morals and ethics decided locally, cultural voices naming their own heritage, difficult conversation better than stagnation) beside a Canada panel on land acknowledgement and the Truth and Reconciliation teaching mandate as a model for filling a gap in national history.

beats.title: What a border does to a qualification
beats.summary: A participant working on a project with migrant women named the challenge the group had not touched: a lawyer in their own country, cleaning houses here. Speaking the local language is a matter of respect and the gate to everything else, they said, since a person cannot live twenty years in a country without it and, without it, college and university stay closed, though keeping one's own culture was never in question. They also named the harder disappointment, arriving in a country that says it is not racist and finding racism anyway, with going back not an option. Ehren Gruber summarized the gap: a professional license or degree stops counting on arrival, a successful life restarts from the bottom, and language itself blocks both the new culture and the next job, so education is needed to close it. Chase Kubic added the soldiers he has met who hold the equivalent of a master's degree and enlisted because nobody would recognize their qualifications, and noted that international agencies exist to credit prior study. Larry posted in the chat that he grew up in New Jersey learning everything there is to know about the Lenape.
beats.pullQuote: It's almost like they're starting their life all over again, and they're trying to build back up and the language barrier itself could be a huge obstacle
beats.slideHint: Challenges slide 'what a border does to a qualification': a three-step drop (qualified professional, unrecognized credential, entry-level work) with language shown as the gate across all three, and a side panel naming credential-evaluation agencies and language leveling as existing remedies.

beats.title: Assimilation, welcome, and a steward for the inquiry
beats.summary: Larry told of a well-educated colleague in the Navy, already speaking three languages while becoming an American citizen, and of shutting down shipmates who said the man did not even speak English. The welcoming instinct of some people in a great land, he said, often makes the immigration experience less than desirable, with each group assuming its rights supersede the next arrivals'. From his own family he traced the cost of speed: German-speaking parents who forbade German in the house so his grandmother would assimilate quickly, and two generations on, a descendant who cannot speak it and has lost the commonality with people of another country or religion. Al Goshi stepped away in the chat. Ehren Gruber then put the call to action, so that the evening's collective knowledge would not simply disperse. Rachel Gruber volunteered to look into how curriculum is developed and whether citizens and parents can be given a voice in what their children are taught. Ehren joined her, saying his thesis in human development sits in exactly that space and was part of the impetus for the group, and kept the team open to others. Hez Jenkins volunteered as well and offered to pass the inquiry on. Larry, declining to speak, wrote instead that part of his own education came from adults who were not technically educators, which Ehren read out and extended to elders and technical experts whose skill should not be dismissed for want of letters after a name.
beats.pullQuote: He speaks 3 languages. You barely speak one.
beats.slideHint: Way Ahead slide: the call to action stated as a continuing inquiry with a shared product that others can add to, the volunteers listed with one line each and the fourth name marked withheld, and a side panel headed 'educators without the title' drawn from the chat.

beats.title: Learning reflection and the fellowship circle
beats.summary: Hez Jenkins posted the closing survey, the learning reflection, into the chat with thanks for the group's participation, and Ehren Gruber put the QR code on screen and left it up rather than rushing anyone. He then opened the fellowship circle, where the floor goes round one last time and silence counts as an offering. Larry, trying to channel his inner Hez by writing his notes first, thanked everyone and pressed his point home: he learned as much from four named colleagues from his service years, whose names are withheld here, as from any year in any classroom. Marcia Lopez said the classroom format holds her attention, but she doubts it has a future, and that stories are how an adult learns best, while wondering what that means for children. A participant thanked the circle for the range of perspectives in a respectful environment. Ehren called the evening an example of what such conversations could look like in communities anywhere without descending into conflict, promised products from it, and named the next Lyceum for the following month. Answering Larry's chat proposal for further discussion, he explained the six-month reflection, when stewards report back on their inquiries and the group weighs in, and listed those carrying this one forward: three named in the room, and a fourth, a family member who was not present, withheld here.
beats.pullQuote: I learn here a lot from stories, and I think, as an adult, that is the best way to learn.
beats.slideHint: Post-Survey slide with the Learning Reflection QR code and a chat-link fallback, then a Fellowship Circle slide naming silence as an offering, then a closing slide with the six-month reflection cycle, the stewards for this inquiry with one place marked withheld, and a placeholder for next month's Lyceum.

inquiries.quote: It almost seems like it's a collective responsibility and a collective call to action.
inquiries.callToAction: The call to action stayed with the whole circle rather than one champion: each participant is asked to find a way to build the community in their own sphere of influence, from inviting someone to a Lyceum to watching for local events where the work can be introduced, and Hez Jenkins will follow up by email. Larry volunteered to forward Ehren's presentation video to his rabbi, a conduit to counterparts in other religious organizations. Ursula Wagner offered to share the conference video with her professor and with further contacts as ideas surface. Ehren Gruber plans to approach the Common Ground Scholar network of clergy to see who is willing to amplify the message in their own communities, and will create social media content from this and earlier Lyceums through the summer. Ehren will add and visualize connections to partner organizations on the website, and Chase Kubic will list past Lyceums there in digestible, searchable form with ways to volunteer. Shinrin-yoku flyers will be redrawn in bright hand-drawn nature art with the nature games named on them. A young participant suggested seeking permission to post nonprofit flyers at a school, and the circle put forward a Praxium podcast and short Lyceum clips as content to make next.

storyboard.logline: After an eight-month pause, a Praxium circle spread from Lima to Los Angeles gave an evening, and then some, to one question: how to grow the learning community.
storyboard.arcNotes: The session opened tightly scripted - norms, pre-survey, land gratitude, introductions - and stayed personal longer than usual because eight months of life had piled up: a retirement, an 80-hour coaching certification, a thesis nearing its end, a family living abroad in Lima. The discussion opened up twice. First when the questions were handed to the young participants at the table, whose answers - a school fundraiser run drawing two hundred people, posters cleared with the school, bright hand-drawn nature pictures, games named on the flyer - reframed outreach from adult marketing into something a child would pick up. Second when Ehren Gruber asked why anyone should have to leave the country for cultural experience, which turned the room inward: Habitat for Humanity in Los Angeles, immigrants already arriving in America, one subway stop between worlds in the Bronx, an older neighbor's steps shoveled in Pittsburgh. Convergence came from Al Goshi's communications-theory frame - person to person, then groups, then broad social media, run simultaneously with tailored messaging - which Ehren adopted explicitly at the close. The last third narrowed to obstacles that are practical rather than ideological: crowded inboxes, complaint without solutions, scarce attention. The call to action was left deliberately undelegated, owned by everyone in their own sphere of influence with follow-up by email, and the closing circle ran past time through vulnerability, similarities over wedges, heart rather than regulation, and the website roadmap. Reviewer notes: speaker labels are unreliable from about @1:45:51 to the end, including the block at @1:50:25, so attribution there was read from context rather than from the label; contributions by the two minors are attributed to "a young participant" and they are not named, and one attendee's health remark and a guest veteran's identifying details were left out.

beats.title: Reopening after eight months
beats.summary: Hez Jenkins opened as guide and secretary of the Praxium Foundation, welcoming the circle to the first Lyceum in about eight months, the last having been in November 2025. He read the structural norms for a shared purpose meeting - every person a peer, every voice welcome, safe and respectful comment, seek commonality while respecting difference - and asked that the young guests present be encouraged to speak. He walked the ninety-minute agenda and noted the question was pre-determined, so no time would go to deliberating what to discuss. A two-question pre-survey went up by QR code asking whether each person needed to be helped, hugged or heard and how the circle could help; answers were read aloud at one table, Ehren Gruber observed that his own responses were no longer anonymous, and Chase Kubic offered a hug across the call.
beats.pullQuote: Hey man, if you need a hug, we can give you a hug, you know?
beats.slideHint: Title slide plus Rules and Structural Norms for 'June Lyceum - 28 June 2026', an agenda strip (pre-survey, present circle, shared understanding, sequence of inquiry, post-survey, closing circle), then the pre-survey QR code with a short link fallback for the chat and both questions spelled out.

beats.title: Present circle and land gratitude
beats.summary: Hez led the opening presence as a deliberate stop to the day's hustle, Monday's meetings and tomorrow's problems, orienting the circle toward place, family, self and children. Standing in for the usual Canadian land acknowledgement, he gave gratitude for the Allegheny, Ohio and Monongahela rivers in Pennsylvania, translated Monongahela as 'fallen banks', and invited each person to consider the heritage of their own ground. He then modeled the shared understanding round himself: Army service, and three months in Europe in support of Ukraine since the last gathering. He defined home as the people he feels connected to rather than a fixed address.
beats.pullQuote: Home means something different to her, but home is just people that I feel connected to.
beats.slideHint: Opening / Present Circle slide: land acknowledgement text naming the Allegheny, Ohio and Monongahela watershed with the 'fallen banks' translation, and the three shared-understanding prompts (cultural background, where you call home, what has happened since the last Lyceum).

beats.title: Lima, young voices, and coaching
beats.summary: Ehren Gruber introduced the group joining from Lima, Peru, where a two-day conference on spirituality and religion in society had just finished, and framed the stay as a chance to build community in Latin America. He then gave the young participants space to introduce themselves in their own words, and one answered the cultural identity prompt by claiming many cultures and putting home wherever the family is. Chase Kubic reported from Texas on completing an 80-hour executive, life and goal-setting coaching course he had first been skeptical of, valuing it for drawing out people's own realizations. He also named Parents in Action as the newest channel, focused on developing children for what is coming, and reported more allies and network since the last Lyceum.
beats.pullQuote: thank you, Hez, for putting this on and creating the space for us to practice the Lyceum as this endeavor for shared purpose
beats.slideHint: Shared Understanding slide: the three prompts small in the corner, a Lima photo strip for the conference on spirituality and religion in society, and a callout box for the two newer channels - coaching (80-hour certification) and Parents in Action.

beats.title: Retirement, service, and a thesis
beats.summary: Larry announced his retirement, recommended it to anyone working toward it, and described taking over maintenance at his synagogue on the grounds that the congregation has plenty of lawyers, doctors and judges but few people who can drive a nail straight. Al Goshi named retired Army life as the strongest thread in a mixed cultural background and said he is still trying to make sense of a lot of uncertainty. An attendee showing only as an unrecognized string of letters was invited to come off mic and turned out to be Ursula Wagner, born in Belize and long settled in Los Angeles, entering the tail end of a thesis on Belizean women and mother-daughter bonding. Every introduction converged on the same answer to where home is.
beats.pullQuote: No matter where I am, my family is where home is.
beats.slideHint: Shared Understanding continued: round-robin name list with one line each, the repeated answer 'home is where the family is' pulled out as a large callout, and a small footnote that a device name hid an attendee until she introduced herself on mic.

beats.title: The map and the question
beats.summary: A colored world map placed the circle across the United States, Europe, the Caribbean and South America, used to make the point that what is a problem for one person may not be a problem for another. Hez walked the sequence of inquiry the evening would follow: theories and concepts, application, sources and inputs, opportunities and challenges, then a call to action. He tied the topic to the Praxium's first annual meeting at the beginning of June, called that a milestone, and set the single question for the night. He noted his own arc from wondering two years ago what he could add to guiding this Lyceum.
beats.pullQuote: how do we grow the Praxium learning community? How do we get more people involved?
beats.slideHint: Two slides: colored world map with attendee locations pinned and the Caribbean inset called out, then Today's Inquiry - 'How do we grow the Praxium learning community?' - with the sequence of inquiry listed down the side as the evening's roadmap.

beats.title: Lived experience and trusted conduits
beats.summary: Chase Kubic argued the message can grow because it is fundamentally about humanity, and that the group's lived experience carries further than theory does; he reported consistently warm reception with no substantive pushback, especially for coaching aimed at veterans moving into civilian communities. Ehren Gruber put the same question to the young participants at the table, asking where they had seen families and community members show up at school rather than only students. One named the Terry Fox run, a lap-based school fundraiser for cancer research drawing roughly two hundred people, which produced the night's first concrete channel: local events and schools. Larry then described discussing the video of Ehren's presentation with his rabbi that day and forwarding it that evening, treating the rabbi as a conduit to counterparts in other religious organizations, while Hez pointed to the existing Facebook and LinkedIn work and short clips cut from Lyceums.
beats.pullQuote: We're tired of sitting in the passenger seat getting told, hey, this is where we're going. No, we want to get in the driver's seat and we want to lead.
beats.slideHint: Theories and Concepts slide: bullets for message rooted in humanity, lived experience over theory, reception to date, veteran transition coaching, and local events and schools as an untapped audience (Terry Fox run, about 200 attendees), with 'driver's seat, not passenger seat' as the banner line.

beats.title: Flyers a kid would read
beats.summary: Ehren asked the young participants how to reach children about the Shinrin Yoku forest bathing offering, a six-month project whose flyers and email lists only reach adults. Their answers were specific: posters put up at school with permission, bright hand-drawn nature pictures instead of adult-oriented documents, and naming the nature games on the flyer so children know games are part of the immersion. Ehren noted that learners in their sixties and seventies already run alongside children at these events, and a further suggestion that the material include everyone led him back to the mission language of fellowship through diversity. Hez Jenkins added mediums beyond social media - a scoreboard advertisement at a Pirates game, radio, a Praxium podcast running interviews - and Ursula Wagner asked permission to share Ehren's conference video with her professor, which he granted without restriction.
beats.pullQuote: if you're talking about making hand-drawn images of things that kids would naturally want to see, you're right
beats.slideHint: Channels and Amplifiers slide: two columns, trusted conduits (clergy, professors, veteran networks, shared video) and mediums (Facebook, LinkedIn, shorts, podcast, radio, event advertising), plus a mock kid-facing Shinrin Yoku flyer - bright colors, hand-drawn nature, games named, multiple generations shown.

beats.title: Framing outward, building in Lima
beats.summary: Hez opened the application section on making a message land outside America, using Pittsburgh dialect ('yinz' where others say 'y'all') and World Cup visitors discovering ranch dressing as examples of how accidentally local a message can be. Ehren described Alternative Peru, the nonprofit Rachel Gruber found, whose guided excursions deliberately skip the standard Cusco and Machu Picchu itinerary. Young participants recounted a week of community building in Lima: homework help and play at a children's library, a dance hall mixing indigenous and Latin music, a meal in a local family's home where the hosts asked what the visitors made of Peru, and a boatyard where they met the man who builds most of the boats. Ehren drew the summarizing point that these are the things residents actually do, and that curiosity and broken Spanish were enough to start the conversations.
beats.pullQuote: we've gone to a children's library to help out with, like, their homework, and we've been playing with them
beats.slideHint: Application slide: 'how is this handled around the world' with the Alternative Peru non-tourist model listed against the standard tourist itinerary, four Lima examples as icons (library, dance hall, shared meal, boatyard), and a caption on messaging that travels past its own dialect.

beats.title: Citizens of the world
beats.summary: Hez described meeting nonprofit organizations while in Europe that act as a central hub between donors and people in need, and using those conversations to introduce the Praxium's work with veterans and across generations. Asked how the family explains ending up in Peru, Ehren said he tells people they are citizens of the world, learning and loving together by doing it physically rather than talking about it. He framed travel as resilience practice and suggested that a family who travels can role model the practice for families who have not considered it. Ursula Wagner and Hez both affirmed the shaping effect of such experience, Hez recalling helping build houses in Mexico and needing a translator to connect.
beats.pullQuote: I've been really telling people that we're citizens of the world, and that we're trying to learn and love together
beats.slideHint: Application continued: 'citizens of the world' as the header, with a three-step ladder (exposure, experience, resilience) and a side panel on nonprofits as donor-to-resource hubs and interconnecting older and younger generations.

beats.title: The next neighborhood over
beats.summary: Prompted by the land acknowledgement being brought home to Pennsylvania, Ehren turned the inquiry inward and asked how to encourage people into a different neighborhood in their own city instead of a foreign country. Hez framed members as ambassadors for a better community and proposed using social media to show where each person is and how they are connected to the land they live on. Ursula Wagner described volunteering with Habitat for Humanity on the west side of Los Angeles and argued that immigrants already arriving in America should be made to feel welcome, because the communities needing help are right here. Hez matched that with shoveling snow and helping older neighbors without vehicles reach appointments through a hard Pittsburgh winter, and Larry with Pelham Parkway in the Bronx, where one subway stop moved you between Jewish, Italian and Chinese neighborhoods.
beats.pullQuote: you really only had to go a subway stop down the way and you were in a different world
beats.slideHint: Application - Cultural exchange at home: reframe banner 'you do not have to leave the country to cross a culture', with three worked examples (Habitat for Humanity in Los Angeles, welcoming immigrants already here, a Bronx subway stop between neighborhoods) and a small prompt asking each attendee to name one neighborhood they have never visited.

beats.title: Three fronts at once
beats.summary: Al Goshi supplied the evening's organizing frame from communications theory: person-to-person engagement as the building block, then groups and affinity groups, then the much broader community reachable through social media. He assessed the Praxium as working mostly person-to-person with some group and social media effect, and argued the three have to run simultaneously, with messaging tailored to each audience while the core message holds. Hez connected that to holding public Lyceums in a commonplace room that needs no Teams link, computer, tablet or internet, where a person can walk in and be helped, heard or hugged. That closed the loop back to the pre-survey question of how each person arrives.
beats.pullQuote: But doing all three simultaneously is probably the most effective way to grow the effort overall.
beats.slideHint: Scaling model slide: three-tier diagram (individual, group and affinity, broad social media) with 'run all three at once, tailor the messaging, hold the core message' beneath, and a side note on in-person public Lyceums with no technology barrier tied back to helped / heard / hugged.

beats.title: Common ground and veterans
beats.summary: Chase Kubic recast the sources question as building the network and the team on top of several years of groundwork, and marketing the group's relevance and impact on communities. Ehren named the Common Ground Scholar collaborative, whose two-day conference drew over two hundred participants including Buddhist, Orthodox Christian, Muslim and Jewish clergy, as a network worth asking to amplify the message in their own communities. He recounted a dinner conversation with a veteran who keeps his military service off his professional profile but volunteered it once the Praxium's message came up, and the W. E. B. Du Bois challenge, written from Ghana, to veterans who fought for democracy abroad; his takeaway was the common ground network plus veterans groups, with service out of uniform as the framing. Ursula Wagner said the conversation kept generating more places she would share the video, Hez pointed to existing small groups such as his Saturday running group as ready-made openings, and Al Goshi called a group run forest bathing on the road.
beats.pullQuote: you fought for liberty abroad, but why can't you do it at home?
beats.slideHint: Sources and Inputs slide: who and what is needed - Common Ground Scholar and interfaith clergy, veteran service organizations, the Kintsugi campaign, existing affinity groups such as running and fellowship groups - with the Du Bois challenge as the pull quote and 'service, just not in uniform' as the framing line.

beats.title: Complaint, universality, and saying hello
beats.summary: Hez described the military family skill of getting a household linked into a community, a religious group or some fellowship on arrival so nobody sits staring at four walls, and noted how much the younger generation struggles to build that kind of connection. He named a habit he sees in military culture and beyond - complaining without solutions - and proposed answering it by asking people how they would actually fix the problem if handed authority for a day, with community as the honest answer. Ursula Wagner held that the human experience is universal wherever you go, the same fear, joy, need for belonging and wanting the best for your family, and only the difficulty varies; she described greeting strangers in the street in her country of birth, missing that for years, and now saying hello first even when nobody answers, because she has done her part. Chase Kubic added that a first hello can open an entire dialogue, and that whatever problem someone is stuck on, somebody out there has already lived it and holds wisdom worth asking for.
beats.pullQuote: most of the time it's more of just complaining without solutions
beats.slideHint: Opportunities slide split in two: on the left the pattern to break (complaint without solutions, four walls on arrival, younger generation out of practice), on the right the low-cost moves (say hello first, ask how they would fix it, assume someone has already solved it), under the header 'the human experience is universal'.

beats.title: Inbox noise and priorities
beats.summary: Hez turned to opportunities and challenges and named communicating meaningfully with people who are all in a hurry as the hardest of them. Larry sharpened it to inboxes full of people demanding attention and competing for time and resources, and asked how anything rises above that noise. Hez answered that no magical filter exists, and that three months away from his phone had shown him how few things actually matter; he retold a lecture demonstration in which golf balls stand for the few big priorities, gravel and sand for everything that fills the gaps, and a poured beer for the room left to have fun. His own practice is writing down a top three and slowing down deliberately - forest bathing, a walk with a podcast, a quiet cup of coffee - and Ursula Wagner said writing things down and forest bathing both work for her.
beats.pullQuote: how do you separate the wheat from the chaff
beats.slideHint: Challenges slide: bullets for attention scarcity, inbox noise, busy schedules and the difficulty of being heard, paired with a jar graphic (golf balls, gravel, sand, beer) and the practices column - top three written down, mindfulness, time in nature.

beats.title: A collective call to action
beats.summary: Rather than naming one champion for the topic, Hez made the call to action collective and said it would come as a follow-up email: each person decides how they will contribute to building the community in their own sphere of influence. He pointed to what the room had already offered - sharing Ehren's video, inviting people to a Lyceum, reaching out locally, posting to social media - and challenged everyone to make the difference where they are. Ursula Wagner answered that she would do it. Ehren Gruber adopted Al Goshi's three fronts explicitly for the summer, noted that families off school spend more time on social media, and committed to creating Lyceum content for the Facebook and LinkedIn presence heading into fall.
beats.pullQuote: it almost seems like it's a collective responsibility and a collective call to action
beats.slideHint: Way Ahead / Call to Action slide: 'In what way can you contribute to building this community?' with the four offers already on the table listed beneath, the follow-up email named as the mechanism, and a summer-into-fall timeline strip for the social media content.

beats.title: Reflection survey and gratitude
beats.summary: The learning reflection questionnaire went out as the last slide, answered anonymously and explicitly not used to track anyone down, with the link dropped into chat for whoever could not scan it. Opening the final round himself, Hez thanked the circle for the chance to guide the evening after eight months apart, and noted who was joining from where, including a family in Peru and a colleague coming off a field rotation. He recalled working with international communities that had drifted from what they could build together toward what they could get out of it, and telling them to imagine instead what they could all do together. He credited the Lyceum's mix of places and experiences for both its camaraderie and its reach, then joked about sour Pittsburgh first impressions and the steel companies that left.
beats.pullQuote: if you could do this by yourself, like, imagine what we could all do together
beats.slideHint: Post-Survey slide: learning reflection QR code with the chat-link fallback, the two prompts (what spoke to you today, what should the next Lyceum take up), a note that answers are anonymous, and a closing-round marker underneath.

beats.title: Vulnerability and shared similarities
beats.summary: Ursula Wagner named pride and the human wish to be seen as good enough as the material the circle is working with, and said the hard part is holding love and vulnerability alongside the work of meeting people where they are; asked to repeat it, he said it again. Ursula Wagner, still working through the questionnaire on a shifted screen, asked forgiveness for being a little technically challenged. Invited to give closing remarks, she picked up Larry's earlier story: two blocks over in New York City is another world, so you do not have to travel around the world to see the world, and much of the change the group wants can happen inside America. Chase Kubic agreed and argued that focusing on similarities and mutual help, rather than driving wedges, is what keeps a collective from breaking into smaller groups that argue and bicker.
beats.pullQuote: you don't have to travel around the world to actually see the world
beats.slideHint: Closing Circle slide one: two facing panels - 'be vulnerable, meet people where they are' and 'similarities over wedges' - with the restated reframe across the bottom, that seeing the world can start two blocks away.

beats.title: Heart, and the website roadmap
beats.summary: Hez observed that when the person in charge is the one handing out division cards, looking past the divisions gets harder, and Ursula Wagner answered that a community should not need laws and regulations to behave decently; Hez named heart for service as the thing underneath. Ursula also said she has been reserved but feels more and more comfortable in her share each time she comes back, and the circle told her it was glad to have her experience and her studies on the calls. Chase Kubic called the group's real contribution the creation of space for dialogue, where people who sit at different points on the political spectrum can air differences without cutting each other's throats, and Hez added that technology has cost some of the younger generation the mannerisms for starting such a conversation. Hez closed on the Praxium's calls to action through the Kintsugi campaign, the Lyceum and social media; Ehren Gruber added the website work on visualizing connections to partner organizations and Chase the plan to list previous Lyceums in a digestible, searchable form with ways for people to volunteer, before thanks and goodnights slightly over time.
beats.pullQuote: We shouldn't need laws and regulations.
beats.slideHint: Final slide pair: the Praxium offerings as calls to action (Lyceum, Kintsugi, Shinrin Yoku, social media), then the website roadmap - partner organization map, searchable archive of previous Lyceums, volunteer sign-up - with a goodnight line and the next Lyceum placeholder.
